Hardy

HAR-dee — sounds like 'hearty' but spelled with a d; hardy things are hard to harm. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Hardy is tough enough to withstand difficult or harsh conditions without being harmed by them.

These hardy little shrubs survive the mountain's freezing winters year after year.

Worked Example

A tiny flower grows on a windswept cliff above the sea. It is blasted by salt spray all summer and buried in frost all winter. Yet every spring, it blooms again.

Something that endures harsh conditions and keeps thriving is hardy. Unlike 'strong,' which suggests raw power, hardy specifically means able to withstand hardship over time.

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

tough

tough: able to endure rough treatment

rugged

rugged: sturdy and able to take hard use

Antonyms

fragile

fragile: easily broken

delicate

delicate: easily harmed or damaged

How Strong Is It? — healthy → hardy → indestructible

healthy vs. hardy

healthy vs. hardy: Healthy is weaker than hardy — a healthy plant is doing well right now, while a hardy one is built to stay well through frost, drought, and abuse.

indestructible vs. hardy

indestructible vs. hardy: Indestructible is stronger than hardy: hardy things survive harsh conditions, but indestructible things cannot be destroyed at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — hard-

root — hard-: bold, hardened (Germanic (via Old French hardi))

suffix — -y

suffix — -y: having the quality of (English)

Put it together

Put it together: Old French hardi meant 'bold,' from a Germanic word meaning 'to make hard.' Something hardy has been toughened — made hard enough to take hardship.

Use the root in a new word: hardship

Use the root in a new word: hardship: The pioneers endured great hardship during the long winter journey.
